sections.h2: Where do you record a deed in Barron County, WI?
sections.html:
Barron County deeds are recorded by the county Register of Deeds, the office that holds both real estate records and vital records for the county. You will find it listed among the departments on the county website.

The office describes its purpose as guarding the official repository of property records and keeping that repository open to the public. Sellers should note one limit: nobody at the counter will run a real estate search for you. The title company or closing agent handles that order. You bring the finished deed to the register for recording.

Under s. 59.43 the register records each document presented that the law permits, marks it with the date, hour and minute, and works through documents in the order received.

A flat $30 covers recording for most documents in Barron County, set by s. 59.43(2)(ag). Whoever requests the service pays up front.

The rest of the state schedule is brief:

  • A deed, mortgage, satisfaction or similar recordable document: $30.
  • A cemetery, subdivision or condominium plat: $50.
  • Copies: $2 for page one, then $1 for every added page, and $1 more for a certification.

Getting your recorded paperwork back takes a little planning. A self-addressed stamped envelope brings a paper copy, and an email address brings a PDF. Without one of the two, the document is not returned, so tuck one into the packet. The Wisconsin Register of Deeds Association posts a recording and filing fee schedule as well.

sections.h2: How much is the Wisconsin transfer fee on a Barron County sale?
sections.html:
The charge is 30 cents per $100 of value on a taxable deed, or $3 per $1,000, and the seller owes it (s. 77.22). Barron County's median owner-occupied home value is $216,600, which gives a sense of the scale for a typical house.

Value means the whole price paid or to be paid, including liens. For a land contract, use the full principal the buyer agrees to pay. Payment goes to the register along with the deed, and both seller and buyer sign the return. Nobody at the register double-checks your stated value or exemption claim, so accuracy is on the signers. Of the fee, the county retains 20 percent and the state receives the balance (s. 77.24).

The return itself is now filed with the Department of Revenue through My Tax Account. Before you log in, collect the completed deed, each party's name, address, phone and email, a Social Security number, ITIN or FEIN for every seller and buyer, and the parcel numbers off the property tax bill.

Once the return is submitted, print the receipt and carry it to the register with the notarized deed and your payment. A few counties accept the packet electronically, so ask the Barron County office which route it prefers. If the property spans two counties, file a return for each. A value understated by 25 percent or more, or a wrongly claimed exemption, brings a penalty of $25 or 25 percent of the added fee, whichever is greater. For questions, email RETR@wisconsin.gov or phone 608-264-6885.

An exemption under s. 77.25 is the only way a deed escapes the fee, and the deed must cite the subsection that applies. For home transfers, the exemptions you are most likely to use cover:

  • passing property by will, descent or survivorship;
  • gifts or nominal-price deals between parent and child, stepparent and stepchild, or grandparent and grandchild;
  • transfers between spouses;
  • foreclosure, or a deed in lieu of foreclosure, running to the mortgage holder;
  • property valued at no more than $1,000;
  • a corrective or confirming deed that repeats an earlier recorded conveyance for nominal or no consideration.

Wisconsin reads exemptions narrowly, and if the return does not offer the one you expected, the transfer owes the fee. A house moving within a family deserves a check of this list before anyone pays a fee that may not be owed.

sections.h2: Deed format rules for Barron County
sections.html:
The register may refuse a deed that misses the standard document format in s. 59.43(2m). Prepare it with these rules in mind:

  • Keep a blank square of at least 3 by 3 inches in the top right of page one for the recording stamp.
  • Place the title in the top 6 inches, with return information on page one.
  • Write down the identification number of every parcel the document touches.
  • Choose white paper of 20 pound weight or heavier, 8.5 inches wide, cut to 11 or 14 inches. No hinged pages.
  • Print in black, blue or red ink. The top margin is half an inch and the other margins a quarter inch.
  • Name whoever drafted the document, and type or print the grantor, grantee and notary names legibly.

Signatures in the original must be notarized or authenticated, and the transfer return and fee or exemption number accompany the deed. Watch for Social Security numbers too. Section 59.43(1m) forbids recording a document that contains one. When related documents are marked as a single transaction and one fails, the register may send back the entire set unrecorded.

sections.h2: Can you record electronically in Barron County?
sections.html:
Yes. The county keeps a page of trusted e-recording submitters, and five vendors appear there: CSC eRecording, EPN (Erecording Partners Network), Indecomm Global Service, Simplifile (a division of ICE Mortgage Technology) and Hopdox.

Find out from your closing agent whether the file will travel through one of these channels or arrive on paper, and confirm with the Barron County register that it will be accepted that way before signing day.

Barron County is mostly rural, with four cities: Barron (the county seat), Chetek, Cumberland and Rice Lake. The population is flat and the share of older residents is high.

Pull the paperwork together ahead of closing day so recording does not hold up the sale. Most of this list repeats points made above:

  • A signed, notarized deed carrying the full legal description. The shortened version on a tax bill will not do.
  • The parcel number from the Barron County tax bill.
  • The receipt from the Real Estate Transfer Return, or the exemption subsection when no fee applies.
  • Cash or a check covering the $30 recording fee plus any transfer fee.
  • A stamped return envelope or an email address for your copy.

The day before closing, ask the closing agent to confirm each item.

A cash buyer skips the lender's underwriting and appraisal, which often shortens the timeline. Recording itself works the same. The deed must still meet the format rules, the transfer return must still be filed, and the fee or exemption must still be settled. With a deed prepared early, a cash closing can be recorded quickly, so check the format list and the return receipt a few days before the date you set.

faqs.q: What does Barron County charge to record a deed?
faqs.a: Thirty dollars under s. 59.43(2)(ag). Plats of subdivisions, condominiums and cemeteries run $50. On top of that, a seller pays the state transfer fee of $3 per $1,000 unless an exemption applies.

faqs.q: Who is billed for the Wisconsin transfer fee?
faqs.a: The seller, as grantor on the deed. Section 77.22 sets 30 cents per $100 of value. Seller and buyer both sign the transfer return, and the register collects at submission.

faqs.q: Does the Barron County Register of Deeds search titles for me?
faqs.a: No, the office offers no real estate searches. Have your title company or closing agent run the search, then bring the finished deed in for recording.

faqs.q: Can a deed with a Social Security number be recorded?
faqs.a: No. Wisconsin law bars a register from recording any document showing an individual's Social Security number (s. 59.43(1m)). Keep the number off the deed. Party identifiers go in separately on the transfer return filed with the Department of Revenue.

faqs.q: How is a recorded deed returned to me?
faqs.a: Include a self-addressed stamped envelope for paper or an email address for a PDF, because recorded real estate documents are returned only on that basis. Copies ordered afterward are $2 for page one and $1 for each page after.
